accuracy.evidence: Book parts and roles match Common Core RI.K.5 (front cover, back cover, title page) and RI.K.6 (author and illustrator and the role of each); point and reason follow RI.1.8 and RI.2.8 (identify and describe the reasons an author gives to support points). The blurb is placed on the back cover and the spine is the bound edge seen on a shelf. Every reason sentence was checked to actually support its point: bees pollinate and make honey, guide dogs and search dogs help people.

misconceptions.evidence: Aims at the mix-ups reported in K-2 classrooms: author versus illustrator (title-page prediction and wrong-tap feedback), the blurb thought to be on the front, and above all calling any true fact a reason ('bees have six legs', 'frogs are green') or offering an opinion ('I like frogs') as a reason. Both appear as tempting options in steps 3 and 5 with feedback that praises the fact before saying why it does not back up the point.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics are specific to this topic: dropping a dealt label onto a front cover, spine, back cover or the blurb box inside it; tapping title, illustrator and author on a drawn title page in a set order; picking supporting sentences under a stated point; sorting dog reasons under two competing points; and joining point plus because plus reason. It shares no mechanic with flagprint's book flip or flagtopic's main-topic sort, and passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each idea by acting: the Blurb label is refused on the front cover with a reason, tapping 'by Ana Reed' when asked for the illustrator explains the author's role, 'Bees have six legs' turns red with 'true, but it does not show bees help', and the because step refuses a true but unrelated fact. The done messages confirm the rule only after the learner has found it.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: the blurb on the front cover, the author drawing the pictures, 'six legs' counting as a reason because it is true, and 'frogs need water because frogs are green' working because it is true. The task-done message names the learner's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with ten distinct m= messages naming the slip: back cover versus front, the spine shows the title small, illustrator versus author, reader versus author, blurb versus title page, page numbers, a true fact that does not back up the point, an off-topic sentence, and last page versus title page.

readability.evidence: Kid text measured FK 0.9 against the family limit of 5.0, with short sentences and concrete actions (turn the book over, open the book, on a shelf you see the spine). Adult text measured FK 7.6 against 10.0 and uses the exact terms: front cover, back cover, spine, blurb, title page, author, illustrator, point and reason. Canvas sentences wrap inside their boxes.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler regex and the 12% duplication gate against all 243 earlier lessons. Each kid paragraph covers one feature set (covers and spine, blurb, title page, point and reasons), and the family tip gives a concrete bedtime routine plus a because sentence frame.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360x640 Android light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots of every step: the front cover, spine and back cover fit side by side at 360 px, the six bee sentences each sit on their own full-width row (font raised to 12 after the first screenshot pass), the two dog points share the width, and every canvas target has a large young-class button below.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone in the walkthrough, with no console errors. Both drags (labels onto the book, reasons onto points) have labelled button alternatives such as 'Put Blurb on: Words on the back', the canvas aria-label reads the current label, request or reason, and success is shown by a tick and text, not colour alone.
